slides.say: You make money decisions every single day, usually without noticing. Financial literacy is simply knowing enough to make those choices on purpose.

slides.h: It's a skill, not a talent
slides.say: Nobody is born good with money. It's a skill, which means anyone can learn it, and the earlier you start, the more it helps.
Everything in this course sits on four ideas: earning money, spending it wisely, saving some, and making it grow.

points: Spending on one thing means not spending on another
The thing you give up is the real cost
slides.say: Every dollar can only be used once. What you give up when you choose something is called the opportunity cost.
Do the warm-up, take the quick quiz, and then let's build your first budget.

lessons.title: Needs vs. wants: building a simple budget

slides.say: A need is something you must have to stay safe, healthy and get to school or work. A want is everything else, however much you love it.

points: A phone is a need. The newest one is a want
slides.say: Some things are both. You may need a phone, but you probably don't need the newest model. Ask what the basic version would cost.
A budget isn't a punishment. It's a plan that tells your money where to go before it disappears.
List what comes in, cover your needs, set a limit for wants, and move something to savings first.
A budget gets better each month. If it doesn't fit, adjust it. Don't throw it away.

points: Give it a price and a date
slides.say: Vague goals don't get funded. Name the thing, find its price and pick a date.
Divide the price by the number of weeks. A $120 goal in twelve weeks is just ten dollars a week.
Move the money the day you get it. What you don't see, you don't spend.
Surprises happen. A small emergency fund keeps one bad day from becoming a debt.
Track your progress where you can see it, and celebrate the halfway point.

lessons.title: How banks work: accounts, debit cards and interest

slides.say: A bank keeps your money safe, and lends some of what everyone deposits to other people, paying you a little interest for the use of yours.
Checking accounts are for everyday spending. Savings accounts are for money you want to keep and grow.
A debit card spends money you already have. It's not credit, and some accounts charge fees, so read the terms.

points: APY is what you earn in a year
slides.say: Interest is the price of using money. When you save, the bank pays you. Compare the APY to find the best deal.
In the US, deposits at insured banks are protected up to the limit. Never share your PIN or passwords.

lessons.title: Intro to investing: stocks, risk and diversification

points: Investing can grow more and can lose
slides.say: Saving keeps money safe. Investing aims to grow it more, but it comes with the chance of losing some.

points: A small piece of a company
slides.say: A stock is a tiny piece of ownership in a company. Its price moves as people's opinions of that company change.

points: Higher possible reward means higher risk
slides.say: Higher possible returns almost always come with higher risk. No one can promise you a profit.

points: Don't put everything in one place
slides.say: Spreading your money across many things means one bad pick can't sink you. Index funds do this for you.
Prices bounce around day to day. Long time horizons and calm decisions beat chasing hype.

lessons.title: Earning money: jobs, paychecks and taxes

slides.say: Teens earn money in many ways, from chores and babysitting to first part-time jobs.
Gross pay is what you earn. Net pay is what lands in your account after taxes and deductions.
Payroll taxes take 7.65 percent. Income tax withholding depends on your W-4, and low earners often owe little or none.
Check hours, rate and deductions. If something looks wrong, ask your employer.
Always budget with your net pay. It's the only number you can actually spend.

lessons.title: Credit and debt: borrowing without getting stuck

slides.say: When you borrow, you pay extra, called interest. APR is the yearly rate.

points: About 7 years, roughly double the cost
slides.say: Paying only the minimum can take years and cost nearly double the purchase price.
Some borrowing can help you build a future. Credit card and payday debt usually just costs.
A credit score shows lenders how reliably you repay. On-time payments matter most.
Buy-now-pay-later splits a price into pieces, but it's still debt. Don't let small payments hide a big total.
Prices tend to rise over time, so the same dollar buys less in the future.
Compounding means you earn interest on your interest, so growth speeds up the longer it runs.
Divide 72 by the rate to guess how many years it takes your money to double.
Starting ten years earlier can mean tens of thousands more, from the same monthly amount.
You don't need much. You need time. Start with whatever you can.

lessons.title: Scams and staying safe with money

slides.say: Scammers target teens with fake packages, too-good jobs and hyped-up stocks.
Pressure, odd payment methods and secrecy are the biggest warning signs.
When something feels off: pause, verify with the real company, and tell someone you trust.
Use strong passwords, switch on two-factor, and never share a one-time code with anyone.
If you get caught, it isn't your fault. Tell a trusted adult and contact your bank fast.

lessons.title: Your money plan: putting it all together

slides.say: Your plan brings the whole course together in one page.
A simple starting split is 50 percent needs, 30 percent wants and 20 percent savings.
Automate what you can so good habits don't depend on willpower.
Review once a month. Small adjustments keep your plan realistic.
Now put it to work. Try the simulation, with play money, and see how you decide.
